static-website.title: Static website
static-website.description: A website whose HTML is prepared before a visit and delivered as page files.

meaning.heading: What static means
meaning.definition: A static website serves prepared HTML pages and related files, including styles, images, and JavaScript. The server does not need to assemble new HTML for that visit.
meaning.analogy: Consider a personal introduction. You put your name, experience, and work into page files, then publish them online. When a reader opens that address, the server delivers the page you already published.
meaning.keyPoint: The key question is when the HTML is generated, rather than whether the page has animations, buttons, or interactions.

how-it-works.heading: What happens when you open the site
how-it-works.intro: Start with a common case: the browser needs to fetch the page and has no cached response it can reuse.
how-it-works.prepare: Prepare the files. An author writes HTML or a build tool generates it in advance, before a reader visits.
how-it-works.deploy: Publish the files. Put HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images on a server that can deliver them.
how-it-works.request: Request the page. A reader opens a URL. The browser requests its HTML, and the server returns the prepared file.
how-it-works.render: Display the page. The browser reads the HTML, loads the styles, images, and scripts it needs, then displays the result and runs interactions.
how-it-works.cache: A real visit does not always download every file again. Browser caches and a CDN can reuse content. A CDN is a service with servers in different places that can deliver content nearby; using one does not determine whether a website is static.

example.heading: A small website example
example.intro: A simple portfolio can consist of these files. You do not need to memorize the code; first understand each file’s job.
example.html: index.html contains the structure and initial content, such as a title, introduction, and button.
example.css: style.css controls fonts, colors, spacing, and layouts for different screens.
example.js: script.js runs in the browser, for example to count button clicks.
example.codeIntro: The HTML can prepare a heading and counter button, then load a script:
example.scriptIntro: The script can update the number on the button inside the browser:
example.change: Clicking the button updates the current page in the browser. It does not rewrite the server’s HTML file, so the website can still be served statically.
example.generated: Static pages do not all need to be written by hand. A static site generator can turn articles and templates into HTML in advance, then publish the generated files.

interaction.heading: Try an interactive static page
interaction.intro: Click the page button and compare the browser count with the HTML response count. Then choose “Visit again” and see which number changes.
interaction.explanation: The first click changes a number in browser memory. “Visit again” simulates receiving the initial HTML again, so this example starts the count at zero. A real site can also save state in the browser and restore it on a later visit.

comparison.heading: Static and dynamic websites
comparison.intro: This comparison concerns how the server supplies HTML. Whether a page can change in the browser is a separate question.

work.label: Server work
work.static: Find and return an existing file
work.dynamic: Run application logic and produce a response

data.label: Data in the HTML
data.static: Usually added during authoring or a build
data.dynamic: Can be read from a database or another source for the request

updates.label: Updating published text
updates.static: Edit files, or rebuild and publish
updates.dynamic: Generate a page from updated data

comparison.mixed: One product can use both approaches: prepare public introduction pages in advance and generate account pages for each request. A static page can also call an API after loading to show current data. A button or screenshot alone cannot tell you how the initial HTML was supplied.

uses.heading: When a static website fits
uses.intro: Consider a static website when the main task is publishing content and most readers can receive the same initial page.
uses.portfolio: Personal sites and portfolios: introduce yourself, show projects, and share contact details.
uses.publishing: Blogs, tutorials, and product documentation: authors publish content that readers browse as pages.
uses.marketing: Product and event pages: display public information, with browser scripts for animation or a calculator.
uses.benefits: Prepared files are often straightforward to cache and distribute. They can also reduce the server logic needed to generate pages. Actual speed and cost still depend on images, scripts, traffic, and hosting.
uses.limits: Login, shared comments, payments, live inventory, and stored submissions require the appropriate services and interfaces. The frontend can still be served statically, but public HTML files alone do not implement those functions.

frozen.title: Does static mean the content never changes?
frozen.body: No. Authors can edit and republish files. Static describes how HTML is supplied for a visit, rather than how often the site is updated.

server.title: Does a static website have no server?
server.body: An online visit still needs a server or CDN to deliver files. You may not need to maintain an application that generates HTML, but the files still need hosting and delivery.

database.title: Can a static site use a database?
database.body: A build can read a database or content management system. The browser can also fetch data through an API. Supplying the initial HTML and fetching later data are separate steps.

security.title: Can frontend files store a secret API key?
security.body: Do not put secret keys in public HTML or JavaScript. Readers can inspect files delivered to their browser. Operations that need secrets should use an appropriate server-side interface.

recap.heading: Check your understanding
recap.question: A portfolio generates all its HTML in advance. It has animations, filter buttons, and a weather API call. Can it still be a static website?
recap.reason: Its initial HTML exists before the visit. Animations, filtering, and later API requests run in the browser; they do not turn the initial HTML into a response generated for that request.
recap.remember: Ask this question: When someone opens the page, does the server return existing HTML or generate HTML for that request?
